stem: Which statement best describes a healthy person?

options.content: A person who is physically, mentally and socially well
options.rationale: Correct: health has all three parts.

options.content: A person who has never needed to visit a clinic
options.rationale: Health is more than not being ill.

options.content: A person who is physically strong and fit
options.rationale: Physical health is only one part of health.

options.content: A person who eats a lot of food every day
options.rationale: Eating a lot is not the same as eating a balanced diet, and diet is only one part of health.

explanation: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.

stem: A person who has no disease is always healthy.
explanation: False. Health also includes mental and social well-being: a person who is free of disease but constantly anxious, or isolated from others, is not fully healthy.

stem: Tendai is physically fit and is never ill, but he spends every break alone, has no friends at school and avoids taking part in class activities. Which part of his health is poor?

options.content: Social health
options.rationale: Correct: he does not mix with or relate to other people.

options.content: Physical health
options.rationale: He is fit and never ill.

options.content: Personal hygiene
options.rationale: Nothing is said about his cleanliness.

options.content: Food hygiene
options.rationale: Nothing is said about how his food is handled.

explanation: Social health is about getting on with other people and taking part in community life. Tendai is physically healthy but socially isolated.
hints: Health has three parts: physical, mental and social. Which one is about relationships with other people?

stem: When is it most important to wash your hands with soap and water?

options.content: After using the toilet and before handling food
options.rationale: Correct: this stops germs from faeces reaching food and the mouth.

options.content: Only when your hands look or feel dirty
options.rationale: Germs are too small to see, so clean-looking hands can still carry them.

options.content: After playing sport and before going to class
options.rationale: Hands must be washed after the toilet and before eating.

options.content: Before going to bed and after waking up
options.rationale: The key times are after the toilet and before handling food.

explanation: Washing hands with soap after using the toilet and before handling or eating food removes pathogens before they can reach food or the mouth.

stem: Why should cooked food at a market stall be kept covered?

options.content: Covering food keeps it warm, which stops bacteria growing.
options.rationale: Warm food lets bacteria multiply faster; the cover is there to keep flies off.

options.content: Covering food stops its vitamins from evaporating into the air.
options.rationale: Vitamins do not evaporate from food; the reason is hygiene.

options.content: Flies that have been on faeces or rubbish can leave bacteria on it.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Sunlight falling on uncovered food turns it poisonous.
options.rationale: Sunlight does not make food poisonous; flies carry bacteria to it.

explanation: Houseflies carry bacteria on their feet and mouthparts from faeces and rubbish to food. Covering food breaks this route of transmission.

stem: Which of these are good food hygiene practices? Select all that apply.

options.content: Using the same unwashed knife for raw meat and bread
options.rationale: This transfers bacteria from raw meat to bread.

options.content: Leaving cooked food uncovered so that it cools faster
options.rationale: Uncovered food attracts flies.

options.content: Washing vegetables in water from an unprotected well
options.rationale: Unsafe water can add pathogens to the food.

options.content: Drying washed plates on a raised dish rack
options.rationale: Correct: plates kept off the ground stay clean.

options.content: Cooking meat thoroughly and eating it while hot
options.rationale: Correct: heat kills bacteria.

options.content: Keeping raw meat away from cooked food
options.rationale: Correct: bacteria on raw meat can spread to food that will not be cooked again.

explanation: Thorough cooking, separating raw and cooked food and keeping clean utensils off the ground all stop pathogens reaching food. Unsafe water, uncovered food and dirty knives spread them.

stem: Diarrhoea from cholera can kill a young child quickly. Name the condition, caused by the loss of water and salts from the body, that is responsible.
explanation: Dehydration: diarrhoea and vomiting remove water and salts faster than the child can replace them.

stem: Mixing bleach with another toilet cleaner makes a safer and stronger disinfectant.
explanation: False. Some cleaning products react with bleach to give off poisonous gases. Use one disinfectant at a time, diluted as the label says, in a well-ventilated place.

stem: Learners clear rubbish out of a blocked drain and then pour disinfectant into it. How does this help to prevent disease?

options.content: The disinfectant makes the drain water safe to drink.
options.rationale: Drain water is never safe to drink.

options.content: It stops the drain smelling, which is the main cause of disease.
options.rationale: Smells do not cause disease; pathogens and vectors do.

options.content: The cleared rubbish can now be burnt to make the air cleaner.
options.rationale: Burning rubbish pollutes the air; the benefit is removing breeding sites and killing pathogens.

options.content: No standing water is left for mosquitoes, and pathogens are killed.
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: A clear drain carries water away instead of letting it stand where mosquitoes breed, and the disinfectant kills germs that multiply in the dirty water.

stem: Which method of waste disposal releases poisonous fumes when the waste contains plastics and rubber?

options.content: Burying in a refuse pit
options.rationale: Buried plastic does not rot, but it does not give off fumes.

options.content: Recycling
options.rationale: Recycling collects plastics to make new products.

options.content: Composting
options.rationale: Plastics are not composted.

options.content: Burning
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Burning plastics and rubber releases poisonous gases and smoke that pollute the air and harm health.

stem: A family plans to dig a refuse pit next to their shallow well because it is close to the kitchen. What is the main danger?

options.content: The pit will fill up with water more quickly near a well.
options.rationale: The distance from the well does not change how fast the pit fills.

options.content: Pathogens and harmful substances may seep into the well water.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Waste cannot rot properly in the damp soil near a well.
options.rationale: Waste rots well in damp soil; that is not the danger.

options.content: Smoke from burning the pit's waste will reach the kitchen.
options.rationale: Smoke may be a nuisance, but the main danger is pathogens reaching the well water.

explanation: Liquid from rotting waste can carry chemicals and pathogens down through the soil into underground water, so refuse pits must be dug well away from wells and boreholes.
hints: Think about where rainwater goes after it falls on the waste in the pit.

stem: A school has a large amount of each kind of waste below. Which is the best to recycle rather than bury?

options.content: Potato peelings from the kitchen
options.rationale: These rot quickly and can be composted or buried.

options.content: Leaves swept from the school grounds
options.rationale: These rot and make good compost.

options.content: Empty aluminium drink cans
options.rationale: Correct: metal does not rot when buried and can be melted down and used again.

options.content: Used paper towels from the toilets
options.rationale: These are soiled and are not suitable for recycling.

explanation: Aluminium cans do not rot in a pit, but they can be collected, melted and made into new cans, saving raw materials and energy.
hints: Which waste would still be in the pit, unchanged, many years later?

stem: Name the government agency that is responsible for protecting the environment in Zimbabwe and can fine people who litter.
explanation: The Environmental Management Agency (EMA).

stem: Match each route of disease transmission with the disease the syllabus links it to.
explanation: Cholera is spread through contaminated water, Ebola through contact with body fluids, malaria by the female Anopheles mosquito and typhoid mainly through contaminated food.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Cholera is spread mainly through contaminated {{blank:a}}, while malaria is carried from person to person by a {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Cholera bacteria are carried in water contaminated with faeces; the malaria parasite is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito.

stem: How does the way a housefly spreads disease differ from the way a mosquito spreads malaria?

options.content: The fly injects bacteria when it bites; the mosquito leaves parasites on food.
options.rationale: This is the wrong way round.

options.content: Flies carry bacteria on their bodies to food; mosquitoes inject parasites.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Both carry pathogens on their legs and leave them on food or skin.
options.rationale: Houseflies do not bite people to feed on blood.

options.content: Flies spread malaria parasites; mosquitoes spread cholera bacteria.
options.rationale: This swaps the diseases: flies carry cholera bacteria to food, and mosquitoes inject malaria parasites.

explanation: A housefly picks up bacteria on its feet and mouthparts from faeces and leaves them on food. The female Anopheles mosquito carries Plasmodium in its body and injects it into the blood when it feeds.
hints: Does a housefly bite people? Where on its body are the germs it carries?

stem: People catch bilharzia when they wade, wash or swim in infected water. Which animal carries the parasite in that water?

options.content: Mosquito larvae
options.rationale: Mosquitoes carry malaria, not bilharzia.

options.content: Freshwater snails
options.rationale: Correct: the larvae leave the snails and burrow through human skin.

options.content: Fish
options.rationale: Fish do not carry the bilharzia parasite.

options.content: Frogs
options.rationale: Frogs do not carry the bilharzia parasite.

explanation: The bilharzia parasite develops in freshwater snails; its larvae leave the snails and burrow through the skin of people in the water.

stem: In a boarding hostel of 120 learners, 18 fell ill with diarrhoea in the same week. What percentage of the learners fell ill?
A secondary school produces food waste from its kitchen, paper from its classrooms and plastic bottles from its tuck shop.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State two advantages of burying the food waste in a refuse pit.

points.description: It is cheap and simple / needs no machinery
Covering it keeps away flies, rats and dogs, or the waste rots and enriches the soil

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State two disadvantages of burning the plastic bottles.

points.description: Burning plastics releases poisonous fumes or smoke that pollute the air and harm health
Fire may spread (veld fire) / carbon dioxide is released / the ash still has to be disposed of

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why recycling is a better way to deal with the plastic bottles than burying them.

points.description: Plastics do not rot, so buried bottles stay in the pit for many years and fill it up
Recycling turns them into new products, saving raw materials and energy (and can earn money)

explanation: Burying is cheap and keeps pests away but uses land; burning plastics gives poisonous fumes and risks fires; plastics do not rot, so recycling them saves resources and pit space.
hints: For each method think about cost, pests, pollution of air and water, and whether the waste rots.

stem: A village draws its drinking water from an unprotected river. Some families have no toilet.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how cholera could spread through this village.

points.description: Faeces of an infected person (from open defecation) are washed into the river
Other people drink the untreated river water (or use it on food) and take in the bacteria

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest two ways in which the families could prevent cholera.

points.description: Boil or chlorinate drinking water, or use a protected borehole
Build and use toilets (latrines) so faeces do not reach the river; or wash hands with soap after the toilet and before food

explanation: Cholera bacteria pass from faeces into water and then into people who drink it. Safe water and proper sanitation break the chain.
hints: Follow the bacteria: where do they leave an infected person, and how do they reach the next person?

stem: A rural school has built a tippy-tap beside its toilets: a container of water tipped by a foot pedal, with soap on a string.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why tipping the container with a foot pedal is more hygienic than tipping it by hand.

points.description: Hands do not touch the container, so germs are not passed from one user to the next

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest why the waste water should drain into a soak pit filled with stones.

points.description: So that no puddle forms where mosquitoes could breed or the ground becomes muddy

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State two times at which learners should wash their hands.

explanation: A tippy-tap lets people wash without touching anything that others have touched, uses little water and should drain into a soak pit so that no stagnant water forms.
hints: Think about what passes germs from one person's hands to the next.
